summary:
Ekiti State operates under Nigeria's national legal framework; the provisions and penalties of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act are carried by the national assessment. What is specific to Ekiti is the documented enforcement and violence inside the state, and it is concentrated in Ado Ekiti, the capital.

On 21 January 2014, days after the SSMPA was passed, Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman, was beaten in Ado Ekiti by six men who told her, 'You will get 14 years in prison.' Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report states she was beaten at least twice over the period. The assault carried the statute's maximum penalty as its threat, naming the term she faced.

Health care inside Ekiti was not usable for her. Unable to attend the state's health services safely, she travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment, a round trip of roughly six hours to obtain care she could not safely reach closer to home.

Police enforcement in the capital appears in the same reporting. In September 2014 a man was arrested at Faguyi bar in Ado Ekiti, his third arrest, and released after two days in detention after 2,000 naira was paid for him and 10,000 naira for a friend. In a separate 2014 case, a 25-year-old man in Ado Ekiti was extorted by a state investigator.

The two documented enforcement cases involve men pursued over same-sex conduct rather than trans identity; the trans-specific incident is the January 2014 assault. The state-level material shows police and a state investigator in the capital extracting payments from men perceived as gay, and a trans woman who could not obtain HIV treatment within Ekiti without risk.
tangentialFactors:
Every Ekiti incident in the source material occurred in Ado Ekiti. No incident from elsewhere in the state appears, so the documented picture covers the capital and leaves the rest of Ekiti unrecorded.

The assault on Debbie was carried out by private individuals, while the two enforcement cases involve police and a state investigator. The threat in the assault nonetheless drew on the national statute's penalty, tying private violence to the legal climate rather than to state action alone.

Care outside the state is the documented route: the trans woman in the 2014 account travelled to Ibadan, in neighbouring Oyo State, rather than to any facility within Ekiti.
localsOnly:
Residents who cannot use Ekiti health services safely face travel out of the state for HIV treatment; the documented case involved a three-hour journey each way to Ibadan.

Release from detention in Ado Ekiti has been conditioned on payment. A man arrested at Faguyi bar in September 2014 was held two days and freed after 2,000 naira was paid for him and 10,000 naira for a friend; the same man had been arrested twice before.

State investigators have extorted money directly from residents: a 25-year-old man in Ado Ekiti was extorted in 2014. Payment, rather than any court process, ended both documented detentions.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Ekiti-specific incident after 2014 appears in the sources. Whether bar-based arrests and extortion by police and state investigators continued through the 2020s in Ado Ekiti or elsewhere in the state is not sourced.

No Ekiti-level counts of arrests, prosecutions or convictions exist in the sources; the two enforcement cases are individual accounts, not a rate.

Whether Ekiti's health facilities now provide HIV or trans-related care without outing risk is not sourced, and no state-level hate-crime or protection provision for Ekiti is recorded.

The outcome of the January 2014 assault is unresolved: the sources do not record any investigation, charge or medical follow-up.
